broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Sets the context for why microbiome modulation is a critical strategy in overcoming ICI resistance.
broader_review_uses.material: Introduction sections detailing primary/acquired resistance rates, limitations of CAR-T and kinase inhibitors, and the need for novel adjuvants.
broader_review_uses.purpose: Background on ICI resistance and current treatment landscape

broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Helps position polysaccharide-based microbiome modulation within the broader spectrum of immunotherapy combinations.
broader_review_uses.material: Section 5.1 comparing polysaccharides with dual checkpoint blockade, TIM-3 targeting, and oncolytic viruses in terms of efficacy and safety profiles.

broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Provides forward-looking perspectives on how technology might overcome current limitations in standardizing microbiome-modulating agents.
broader_review_uses.material: Sections 6.3-6.6 discussing AI-driven QSAR, graph neural networks, synthetic biology, and large-scale N-glycomics.
broader_review_uses.purpose: Technological innovations in glycomics and biomanufacturing

facet_contributions.boundaries: Most evidence is preclinical (mouse models) or from small early-phase human trials; causal links in humans are inferred from FMT experiments and observational cohorts.
facet_contributions.contribution: Details the role of gut microbiota in mediating ICI response, specifically highlighting how polysaccharides remodel microbial composition (enriching Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium) and metabolite profiles (increasing SCFAs like butyrate and propionate) to enhance anti-tumor immunity.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Can be used to explain the mechanism by which dietary or supplemental polysaccharides sensitize cold tumors to ICIs via microbiota-dependent pathways.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Mechanisms are often derived from in vitro or syngeneic mouse models; direct translation to human clinical outcomes is not fully validated.
facet_contributions.contribution: Elaborates on the molecular mechanisms of polysaccharide-mediated immunomodulation, including TAM repolarization (M2 to M1), CD8+ T cell exhaustion reversal, and suppression of tumor-intrinsic escape (PD-L1 downregulation). Links these to specific structural motifs (triple helix, acetylation).
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Provides mechanistic depth for how adjuvants reverse ICI resistance, offering specific pathways (e.g., STAT3/galectin-3, Dectin-1/Syk/NF-kB) to cite when discussing non-microbiota mechanisms.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Based on specific dysbiotic mouse models; human relevance requires further validation.
facet_contributions.contribution: Discusses the safety boundaries and risks associated with polysaccharide/fiber supplementation, noting that excessive fermentation in dysbiotic guts may lead to adverse outcomes like cholestatic liver cancer.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Useful for discussing the limitations and risks of microbiota-targeted therapies, providing a balanced view beyond just efficacy.

paper_identity.title: Natural polysaccharides as immune adjuvants to overcome immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance: mechanistic insights, clinical evidence, and translational challenges

planning_summary: This review serves as a critical resource for understanding how natural polysaccharides modulate the gut microbiome to influence ICI efficacy in solid tumors. It provides detailed mechanistic insights into the bidirectional crosstalk between polysaccharide-derived metabolites (SCFAs, indole derivatives) and host immunity, along with a structured analysis of translational challenges and future technological interventions.
scope_interpretation_cautions: The review focuses on natural polysaccharides; do not generalize findings to all prebiotics or dietary fibers without specifying the polysaccharide type.
Clinical evidence is primarily from early-phase trials or real-world retrospective studies; avoid overstating efficacy as if confirmed by Phase III RCTs.
Mechanistic claims are largely supported by preclinical models; distinguish between observed associations in mice and validated causal mechanisms in humans.
Safety warnings (e.g., liver cancer risk) are based on specific dysbiotic conditions; do not assume universal toxicity.
